about: The tea trade of the isles (roadmap C2, 2026-10-23): tea merchants, firms and tea rooms placed at their first shop or works where the source names it, each with sources and exact quotes (checked by python -m bidb.evidence --check). Leads came from George's tea_explorer project; every fact here is from the cited source. Entries with listed_in are kept in that list and only shown here.

entries.name: Jacksons of Piccadilly
entries.claim: tea house and grocer, said to be founded by Robert Jackson in 1700
entries.evidence: The 1700 date is the firm's tradition and no contemporary record of it was found; the Survey of London records the shop front at No. 171 made for Jackson's in 1935. The brand now belongs to Twinings.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Jacksons of Piccadilly
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: founded by Robert Jackson in Piccadilly in 1700

sources.title: Wikipedia: Jacksons of Piccadilly
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: By 1905, Jacksons had moved to 171–172 Piccadilly.

sources.title: Survey of London vols 29-30, St James Westminster pt 1: Piccadilly, South Side
sources.author: F. H. W. Sheppard (ed.), London County Council 1960 (British History Online)
sources.quote: 171 was inserted in 1935 for Jackson's the grocers and tea suppliers

entries.name: Horniman's Tea
entries.claim: John Horniman's tea business, the first to sell tea in sealed packets of known weight and brand
entries.evidence: Founded by John Horniman at Newport in 1826 and moved to London in 1852 to be near the bonded warehouses of the London Docks; by 1891 the largest tea business in the world. Sold to J. Lyons in 1918. Frederick Horniman's fortune built the Horniman Museum.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Hornimans
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: was founded in 1826 in Newport, Isle of Wight, by trader John Horniman

sources.title: Wikipedia: Hornimans
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 1852, he moved the company to London to be closer to the bonded warehouses of London Docks

sources.title: Wikipedia: Mazawattee Tea Company
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: had been introduced in 1826 by John Horniman, who hit on the idea of packaging tea

entries.name: Tetley
entries.location: Huddersfield (the brothers' salt trade, 1822); London from 1856
entries.claim: Yorkshire tea merchants; the first to sell tea bags in the United Kingdom (1953)
entries.evidence: Joseph and Edward Tetley sold salt from a pack horse in Huddersfield from 1822 and set up as tea merchants in 1837 (the town of the 1837 firm is not stated in the source; placed at Huddersfield); the firm moved to London in 1856. Owned by Tata since 2000.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Tetley
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 1822, brothers Joseph and Edward Tetley sold salt from a pack horse in Huddersfield

sources.title: Wikipedia: Tetley
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: they set up as "Joseph Tetley & Co." tea merchants in 1837

sources.title: Wikipedia: Tetley
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Tetley was the first company to sell tea in tea-bags in the United Kingdom in 1953.

entries.name: Bewley's
entries.location: Dublin (placed at the Grafton Street café, 1927)
entries.age_text: tea trade from 1835; company 1840; cafés from 1894
entries.claim: Dublin Quaker tea and coffee merchants
entries.evidence: Samuel Bewley and his son Charles landed a cargo of tea direct from Canton in 1835; the company dates itself from 1840. Cafés followed in South Great George's Street (1894), Westmoreland Street (1896) and Grafton Street (1927).

sources.quote: located in Dublin and founded in 1840

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bewley's
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: in 1835, Samuel Bewley and his son Charles landed 2,099 chests of tea shipped from Canton in China

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bewley's
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The flagship Grafton Street café was opened by Ernest Bewley in 1927.

entries.name: Brooke Bond
entries.claim: Arthur Brooke's tea business; maker of PG Tips
entries.evidence: Arthur Brooke opened his first teahouse at 23 Market Street, Manchester, in 1869; the firm launched Pre-Gest-Tea (PG Tips) in 1930, which led the British market by 1958.

sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 1869, he opened his first teahouse at 23 Market Street, Manchester.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Brooke Bond
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Brooke Bond's most famous brand is PG Tips, launched under the name Pre-Gest-Tea in 1930.

sources.title: Wikipedia: PG Tips
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: By 1958, PG Tips had risen from fourth to first place in the British tea market.

entries.name: Lipton
entries.claim: Thomas Lipton's grocery chain and tea brand
entries.evidence: Thomas Lipton opened his first provision shop at 101 Stobcross Street, Glasgow, in 1871; with some 300 shops he entered the tea trade in 1888 and bought tea gardens in Ceylon in 1890. The brand is now Dutch-based.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Thomas Lipton
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The following year he opened his first provision shop—Lipton's Market—at 101 Stobcross Street in the Anderston area of Glasgow.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Thomas Lipton
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 1888, when his empire had grown to 300 stores, he entered the tea trade and opened his tea-tasting office.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Lipton
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 1890 Lipton purchased tea gardens in Ceylon

entries.name: Whittard of Chelsea
entries.evidence: Walter Whittard opened a tea shop in Fleet Street in 1886; the firm stayed in his family until 1973.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Whittard of Chelsea
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The company was started by Walter Whittard, who opened a tea shop in Fleet Street in 1886

entries.name: Taylors of Harrogate
entries.location: Harrogate (based in the first Bettys tea room)
entries.claim: tea and coffee blenders; makers of Yorkshire Tea
entries.evidence: Charles Edward Taylor and his brother founded CE Taylor & Co. in 1886; Bettys bought the firm in 1962 and launched Yorkshire Tea in 1977, the best-selling tea brand in Britain from 2019. The source does not say where the firm began; placed at its Harrogate home.

sources.quote: Taylors of Harrogate is based in Harrogate, Yorkshire, in the first Betty's tea room.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Yorkshire Tea

sources.quote: It became the best-selling tea brand in Britain in 2019.

entries.name: Mazawattee Tea Company
entries.age_text: Densham firm from 1860s; Mazawattee 1887; Tower Hill building by 1894, bombed 1940
entries.claim: one of the most advertised Victorian tea firms; an early seller of packet Ceylon tea
entries.evidence: The Densham family's wholesale tea firm registered the Mazawattee name in January 1887 and built offices, warehouses and vaults at Tower Hill by 1894; the building was wrecked by bombing in 1940 and its cellars survive as Tower Vaults.

sources.author: Wikipedia contributors

sources.title: Wikipedia: Mazawattee Tea Company
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors

sources.title: Wikipedia: Mazawattee Tea Company
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: in late 1940 the Tower Hill building was bombed and wrecked

entries.name: Barry's Tea
entries.evidence: Founded by James J. Barry in Cork in 1901 and sold from a shop in Prince's Street until the 1960s, when the firm turned to wholesaling.

entries.name: Typhoo
entries.location: Birmingham (the Sumners' shop; street not given)
entries.claim: tea launched by John Sumner Jr. in his family's Birmingham shop
entries.evidence: William Sumner and his son John founded a pharmacy and grocery business in Birmingham in 1870; John Sumner Jr. launched Typhoo there in 1903. Production moved to Moreton, Wirral, in 1978. Placed in central Birmingham.

entries.name: Kardomah (Vey Brothers)
entries.claim: Liverpool tea dealers whose Kardomah cafés spread across Britain
entries.evidence: The Vey Brothers began as tea dealers and grocers in Pudsey Street, Liverpool, in 1844; the Kardomah brand was first served at the Liverpool exhibition of 1887 and later named a chain of cafés.

entries.name: Aerated Bread Company tea shop
entries.location: courtyard of Fenchurch Street station, London
entries.age_text: tea shop 1864; tea rooms from the 1870s
entries.claim: the A.B.C. chain, whose tea rooms were among the first in London
entries.evidence: The Aerated Bread Company (1862) opened a shop selling tea in the courtyard of Fenchurch Street station in 1864, followed by tea rooms in the 1870s.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Aerated Bread Company
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: opening a shop selling tea in the courtyard of London's Fenchurch Street Railway Station in 1864

sources.title: Wikipedia: Aerated Bread Company
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors

entries.name: Lyons teashops
entries.location: Piccadilly, London (first teashop; number not given)
entries.claim: J. Lyons & Co.'s chain of about 200 teashops
entries.evidence: J. Lyons & Co. (1884) opened its first teashop in Piccadilly in 1894 and from 1909 built a chain of about 200; it bought Horniman's in 1918 and Tetley in 1973.

sources.title: Wikipedia: J. Lyons and Co.
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 1894 the company started a teashop in Piccadilly, London, and from 1909 developed this into a chain of teashops which would ultimately number around 200 locations.

sources.title: Wikipedia: J. Lyons and Co.
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 1918, to increase sales in northern England, Lyons bought the old established tea company Horniman & Sons.

entries.name: Bettys Café Tea Rooms
entries.claim: Frederick Belmont's tea room, the first of the Bettys chain
entries.evidence: Frederick Belmont, a Swiss confectioner, opened the first Bettys tea room in Harrogate in 1919.
